title: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
author: Jake Pearson
content:
Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox
with some bad news.

“Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the
message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were
hoping for but this decision is final.”

I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my
balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it
something I’d said?

In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting
companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal
guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of
control are firm enough. For that piece, [I’d intentionally bet like a problem
gambler](https://www.propublica.org/article/draftkings-sports-gambling-
problem-vip-fanduel), recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks.
My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors,
recovering addicts and addiction specialists.

As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me
my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took
three weeks and about $6,000 of losses.

## [What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find
Out.](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-uploader)

If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica
understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your
betting history, then upload your files.

[Share Your Experience](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-
uploader)

The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off
of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts
designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down.
But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this
system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”  

So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a
core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other
hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.

In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer,
Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to”
in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course
of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication,
DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, [telling a CNBC
journalist](https://www.youtube.com/live/T-lCFnIuZnc?si=RxlA5qgM4Y_oE4m8&t=17507)
that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty
proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting,
but I’ve already addressed that [on
X](https://x.com/JakePearsonProP/status/2113673164362535282).)

So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed,
exactly?

DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for
94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my
investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators
and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A [27-minute,
behind-the-scenes documentary](https://www.propublica.org/article/sports-
betting-problem-gambling-draftkings-fanduel) of our work that we posted on
YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three
weeks.

### Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment

Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica

The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps
not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in
the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were
young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage,
leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about
the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story.

Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when
announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how
DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state
officials were also [demanding answers about how the company lures in its
customers and keeps them in the
action](https://www.propublica.org/article/sports-betting-impact-louisiana-
ohio-congress). In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the
apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my
piece.  

On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for [a
story about that impact](https://www.propublica.org/article/sports-betting-
impact-louisiana-ohio-congress).

That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my
account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a
formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations
and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that
the company improperly targets losing gamblers.

I may no longer be able to access my account, but I'm still reporting on
DraftKings and the online gambling industry.

In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better
understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by
[submitting your data here](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-
uploader/?_gl=1*1fimhh0*_ga*NjQyMzE3OTg2LjE2ODgwNDk3NTk.*_ga_K9RW8M6GL5*czE3OTM4MTg5NTckbzExMjIkZzAkdDE3OTM4MTg5NTckajYwJGwwJGgw).
If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and
[jake.pearson@propublica.org](mailto:jake.pearson@propublica.org).
